title: condition on __SANITIZE_ADDRESS__ not being defined?
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/610a26ca8929972e79d56b38b13b37b8658b4ed0/src/init.c#L46-L50

Updating {processx} (3.8.6 -> 3.9.0) broke our internal ASAN build of the package:

```
(01:57:05) ERROR: ...processx/BUILD:76:12: Compiling .../processx/processx/src/init.c failed: (Exit 1) wrapped_clang failed: error executing CppCompile command (from cc_library rule target ...processx:processx.so_deps/processx.so) .../crosstool/v18/stable/toolchain/bin/wrapped_clang '-frandom-seed=blaze-out/k8-opt-asan/bin/.../packages/processx/_objs/processx.so_deps/processx.so/init.pic.o' -iquote . -iquote ... (remaining 290 arguments skipped).
.../packages/processx/processx/src/init.c:49:9: error: '__SANITIZE_ADDRESS__' macro redefined [-Werror,-Wmacro-redefined]
   49 | #define __SANITIZE_ADDRESS__         // GCC already sets this
      |         ^
<built-in>:369:9: note: previous definition is here
  369 | #define __SANITIZE_ADDRESS__ 1
      |         ^
1 error generated.
```

I'm not sure how unique our setup is here, but it does seem harmless to add an `#if !defined(__SANITIZE_ADDRESS__)` in this branch.

title: Timeout systematically too early on Linux
description:
There appears to be a bug on linux where a process’s timeout is consistently biased: the process is terminated too early by a sub-second offset that remains constant during a single boot but changes after rebooting.

Using this example, I got rough values for the actual time till a timeout from 5 different reboots of my system:
```R
replicate(10, {
  start_time <- Sys.time()
  processx::run("sleep", "10", timeout = 3, error_on_status = FALSE)
  end_time <- Sys.time()
  difftime(end_time, start_time, units = "secs")
})
# Boot 1: 2.672711 2.667453 2.670226 2.670044 2.670001 2.672757 2.668645 2.669582 2.669642 2.669321
# Boot 2: 3.002664 2.976912 2.980564 2.979576 2.979316 2.984085 2.977271 2.979840 2.979048 2.981039
# Boot 3: 2.609917 2.586380 2.590400 2.590042 2.590023 2.591098 2.588827 2.589941 2.589849 2.590309
# Boot 4: 2.138885 2.106352 2.108275 2.106977 2.100902 2.111049 2.109790 2.110651 2.108229 2.110446
# Boot 5: 2.629206 2.606612 2.610635 2.609579 2.610023 2.620473 2.609882 2.610334 2.609502 2.610581
```

This is what @mb706 and I could figure out:
Internally, the timeout is determined by `Sys.time() - start_time > timeout` in `run_manage()`: 
https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/6a16b63ec65efaa94d597182885e6b9d7c94f506/R/run.R#L410-L414
with `start_time` ultimately getting defined here:
https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/6a16b63ec65efaa94d597182885e6b9d7c94f506/src/create-time.c#L183-L196

Here, `ct` gets read from the field `starttime` in `/proc/<pid>/stat` and `bt` seems to get defined through `ps::ps_boot_time()` in `.onLoad()`, which reads the `btime` field in `/proc/stat`.
However, the boot time in `/proc/stat` is [**only accurate in seconds**](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_stat.5.html).
If this is rounded down, that would explain why `processx` would think the process is older than it actually is.

This might also relate to this issue: https://github.com/r-lib/processx/issues/394

title: Add ability to get run time duration for `callr::r_bg`
description:
I'd like to be able to run `callr::r_bg()` and then get the duration of time it took to run func, or at least time from opening the R session to it being killed if its too difficult to get timing for the func itself. 

One can get the start time with `x$get_start_time()`, but there is no way that I can see to get the end time. Right now as a hack I do:

```r
library(callr)
x <- r_bg(function() { Sys.sleep(5); "1 done" })
x$wait()
end_time <- as.POSIXlt(Sys.time(), tz = "GMT")
start_time <- x$get_start_time()
as.numeric(end_time - start_time) # duration
```

let me know if I should instead open this in `processx` repo

title: Kill processes on unload, on Windows
Put background job output on the RStudio job pane
description:
poc on Unix:

```r
unlink("/tmp/fifo")
system("mkfifo /tmp/fifo")
script <- quote({
  conn <- processx::conn_create_file("/tmp/fifo")
  repeat {
    out <- processx::conn_read_chars(conn)
    if (nchar(out) == 0) break
    cat(out)
  }
})
cat(deparse(script), file = "/tmp/script.R", sep = "\n")
id <- rstudioapi::jobRunScript("/tmp/script.R")
id

pp <- processx::process$new(
  "bash",
  c("-c", "for i in `seq 1 100`; do sleep 1; echo $i; done"),
  stdout = "/tmp/fifo"
)

# Now you can even do these and more
pp$suspend()
pp$resume()

# rstudioapi::launcherControlJob(id, "kill")
rstudioapi::jobRemove(id)
```

API can be `stdout = "|rstudio"` or we can even have a new function that does this, and inherit from `process` and add methods to manage the rstudio job. But then it will no work for the other subclasses, like `r_process`.

title: Unnable to read more than 78643 chars from stdout pipe
description:
When running a process I seem to unable to read more than 78643 chars.

If I use read_output_lines() I get no result and when I use read_output() it only reads the first 78,643 chars. I think read_output_lines() is not reaching the \n at the end of the line so it doesn't return anything.

After reading with read_output() I cannot read the rest of the line until I send new input. I have tried to troubleshoot with the R debugger but as the read happens through the dll file I can't see what's happening.

The below creates and runs a cmd file to write 100,000 chars, but processx only reads 78,643. It then does the same for 50,000 chars and it reads all 50,000 and prints a summary at the end.

This is on Windows 10 & 11

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(processx)
rm(list = ls())

# Set file names to save to, and if + how long to wait
print_file <- 'to_print.txt'
print_file_2 <- 'to_print_2.txt'
cmd_file <- 'do.cmd'
cmd_file_2 <- 'do_2.cmd'
do_wait <- T
wait_secs <- 2

# Write a text file of 100,000 'a' ending a new line, this will be printed. Make a second with 50,000 chars
'a' %>% rep(100000) %>% paste0(collapse = '') %>% paste0(., '\n') %>% write_file(file = print_file)
'a' %>% rep(50000)  %>% paste0(collapse = '') %>% paste0(., '\n') %>% write_file(file = print_file_2)

# Write a cmd file that prompts for input, then prints the contents of the text file created above
paste0('@echo off \n:prompt\n set /p id="" \ntype ', print_file   , '\nset /p id=""') %>% write_file(cmd_file)
paste0('@echo off \n:prompt\n set /p id="" \ntype ', print_file_2 , '\nset /p id=""') %>% write_file(cmd_file_2)

if(exists('my_proc')){my_proc$kill()}
my_proc <- process$new(cmd_file, stdin = '|', stdout = '|', stderr = '|')

# Feed in \n to begin printing. Try and read output_lines, then just lines. 
# Repeat to try and catch any remaining chars not read
my_proc$write_input('\n')
if(do_wait){Sys.sleep(wait_secs)}

a_output_lines_1_1 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
b_output_1_1 <- my_proc$read_output()
c_output_lines_1_2 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
d_output_1_2 <- my_proc$read_output()

# The above only reads 78,643 chars, which is less than the 100,000 that should be printed
# The remaining 12,357 can be read if you feed in additional input
my_proc$write_input('-')
if(do_wait){Sys.sleep(wait_secs)}

e_output_lines_2_1 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
f_output_2_1 <- my_proc$read_output()
g_output_lines_2_2 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
h_output_2_2 <- my_proc$read_output()

# Collect all the output vars and their lengths into a table
results <- ls() %>% str_subset('output') %>% 
  map(~list(var = .x, length = .x %>% get %>% nchar %>% append(0) %>% pluck(1),
            has_linebreak = .x %>% str_detect('\n'),
            chars = .x %>% get %>% str_extract_all(pattern = '.') %>% unlist %>% unique() %>% paste0(collapse = ''))) %>%
  bind_rows()
# Clear output vars for next run
rm(list = ls() %>% str_subset('output'))

################
##### Part 2
##### Same as above but with 50,000 chars printed
################

if(exists('my_proc')){my_proc$kill()}
#> [1] FALSE
my_proc <- process$new(cmd_file_2, stdin = '|', stdout = '|', stderr = '|')

# Feed in \n to begin printing. Try and read output_lines, then just lines. Repeat to try and catch any remaining chars not read
my_proc$write_input('\n')
if(do_wait){Sys.sleep(wait_secs)}

a_output_lines_1_1 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
b_output_1_1 <- my_proc$read_output()
c_output_lines_1_2 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
d_output_1_2 <- my_proc$read_output()

# All 50,000 char are read on the first try
my_proc$write_input('-')
if(do_wait){Sys.sleep(wait_secs)}

e_output_lines_2_1 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()
f_output_2_1 <- my_proc$read_output()
g_output_lines_2_2 <- my_proc$read_output_lines()

  map(~list(var = .x, length = .x %>% get %>% nchar %>% append(0) %>% pluck(1),
            has_linebreak = .x %>% str_detect('\n'),
            chars = .x %>% get %>% str_extract_all(pattern = '.') %>% unlist %>% unique() %>% paste0(collapse = ''))) %>%
  bind_rows()


results

title: Document common options for output encoding of Windows tools
description:
Create some output with non-ASCII characters, e.g. this on German or Fresh Windows:
```r
res <- processx::run("systeminfo", c("/FO", "csv"), encoding = "windows-1252")$stdout
substr(res, 2200, 2300)
#> [1] "5d4\",\"Es wurde ein Hypervisor erkannt. Features, die f\u0081r Hyper-V erforderlich sind, werden nicht ange"
```

So the `\u0081` is not converted, apparently, even though that seems to be the default encoding:

```
❯ [System.Text.Encoding]::Default


IsSingleByte      : True
BodyName          : iso-8859-1
EncodingName      : Westeuropäisch (Windows)
HeaderName        : Windows-1252
WebName           : Windows-1252
WindowsCodePage   : 1252
IsBrowserDisplay  : True
IsBrowserSave     : True
IsMailNewsDisplay : True
IsMailNewsSave    : True
EncoderFallback   : System.Text.InternalEncoderBestFitFallback
DecoderFallback   : System.Text.InternalDecoderBestFitFallback
IsReadOnly        : True
CodePage          : 1252
```

This might be some `systeminfo` or Windows thing, because according to https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows-1252 `\x81` should be unused:
> According to the information on Microsoft's and the Unicode Consortium's websites, positions 81, 8D, 8F, 90, and 9D are unused; however, the Windows API [MultiByteToWideChar](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/dd319072.aspx) maps these to the corresponding [C1 control codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C0_and_C1_control_codes). The "best fit" mapping documents this behavior, too.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windows-1252#cite_note-bestfit-15)

However, `850` seems to work well:
```r
res <- processx::run("systeminfo", c("/FO", "csv"), encoding = "850")$stdout
substr(res, 2200, 2300)
#> [1] "5d4\",\"Es wurde ein Hypervisor erkannt. Features, die für Hyper-V erforderlich sind, werden nicht ange"
```

title: A question about `PROCESSX_INTERRUPT_INTERVAL`
description:
This value is hardcoded here:

https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/6a16b63ec65efaa94d597182885e6b9d7c94f506/src/processx.h#L78

Is my understanding correct that this interval is there only to allow the interruption of the polling and in no way adds a (significant, i.e. proportional to its value) delay to the time it takes for, let's say, `p$poll_io(-1)` to return?

AFAIU `processx` leverages native libraries to provide overhead-less IO event forwarding (modulo interruptability). See:
- UNIX: https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/6a16b63ec65efaa94d597182885e6b9d7c94f506/src/processx-connection.c#L1965

```
An error occurred when writing to the named pipe. (system error 232, The pipe is being closed.

in process

I may well be doing something wrong. Any thoughts?

title: get_id() subtly alters the session randomization state
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/95ba3aa23262e33b95a1b43dfea822c36589eda3/R/utils.R#L198

Started way upstream as https://github.com/r-lib/pkgload/issues/272 and then https://github.com/r-lib/pkgbuild/issues/185, but the issue traces back to the above -- while trying to build a package, {processx} generates this random ID which messes with the randomization state of the session.

I don't see this documented as intended behavior, so I'm wondering if this is unintentional & perhaps `get_id()` should be careful to restore the randomization state on completion; of course this means consecutive runs of {processx} may generate sessions with the same ID --> not desirable, so maybe the caller needs to deal with this & {processx} just needs to document the issue?

Alternatively, maybe `get_id()` could use the `tempfile()` randomization to generate the IDs, since `tempfile()` does not touch the R-level randomization state?

title: R setting LD_LIBRARY_PATH causes problems in Julia
description:
TL;DR: Setting `env = c("current", LD_LIBRARY_PATH = "")` can help.


### Description

R sometimes sets the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable, which is then inherited by subprocesses. This can cause issues for some Julia packages when Julia is called from R. Here I'm demonstrating Plots.jl, but it happens with others too. (Plots.jl is not installed by default. Julia will prompt you to install if it's not available.)


```r
Sys.getenv("LD_LIBRARY_PATH")
#> [1] "/usr/lib/R/lib:/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu:/usr/lib/jvm/default-java/lib/server"
Sys.getenv("R_LD_LIBRARY_PATH")
#> [1] ""

processx::run("julia", c("--project=.", "-E", "using Plots"))
#> Error in `processx::run("julia", c("--project=.", "-E", "using Plots"))`:
#> ! System command 'julia' failed
#> ---
#> Exit status: -11
#> Stderr:
#> ERROR: InitError:
#> ---

processx::run("julia", c("--project=.", "-E", "using Plots"), env=c("current", LD_LIBRARY_PATH=""))
#> $status
#> [1] 0

```


### system2

`base::system2()` has the same issues as processx, though with `system2`, setting `LD_LIBRARY_PATH=""` doesn't seem to solve things. (I have not dug into this.)

<details>

<summary>
system2 equivalent
</summary>

```r
system2("julia", c("--project=.", "-E", '"using Plots"'))
#> ERROR: InitError: could not load library "~/.julia/artifacts/466e859891e85a1f8a887e712f17b1645ec9c803/lib/libQt6Concurrent.so"
#> /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libQt6Core.so.6: version `Qt_6.5' not found (required by ~/.julia/artifacts/466e859891e85a1f8a887e712f17b1645ec9c803/lib/libQt6Concurrent.so)
#> Stacktrace:
#>   [1] dlopen(s::String, flags::UInt32; throw_error::Bool)
#>     @ Base.Libc.Libdl ./libdl.jl:117
#>   [2] dlopen(s::String, flags::UInt32)

```

</details>


### Platform:

* Ubuntu 23.10
* R 4.3.1

I don't have any of the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`s set outside of R:

```sh
echo "LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$LD_LIBRARY_PATH"
#> LD_LIBRARY_PATH=

#> R_LD_LIBRARY_PATH=

This is not actually a problem with processx, but I thought I should document it here, in case it saves someone else some time. The only change processx could make is to remove LD_LIBRARY_PATH by default, but that's not worth the risk of breaking other things.

title: Process hangs when using pipes with `stdout`, `stderr` for `latexmk -pdf` compilation
description:
I am attempting to orchestrate and keep track of dozens of `latexmk` compilation processes, and noticed that these processes never finish if I attempt to capture `stdout` or `stderr` with pipes.
It works when I log to temp files and read the contents back though, and I don't understand what's going on there.

Consider this minimal `test.tex` file:

```tex
\documentclass{article}

\begin{document}
Hello
\end{document}
```

## Setting `stdout` and `stderr` to temp files 

Works (mostly) as intended:

```r
stdout_file <- tempfile()
stderr_file <- tempfile()

# Cleanup for next run
pc <- processx::process$new(command = "latexmk", args = c("-C"))
pc$wait()
if (file.exists("test.pdf")) file.remove("test.pdf")

p <- processx::process$new(
  command = "latexmk", args = c("-pdf", "test.tex"),
  stderr = stdout_file,
  stdout = stderr_file,
  echo_cmd = TRUE
)

p$wait()
p$get_exit_status()

```

Unfortunately all the output appears to be in `stderr`, but that's just a `latexmk` thing I assume

```
readLines(stdout_file)
character(0)
readLines(stderr_file)
 [1] "Rc files read:"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
 [2] "  NONE"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
[truncated for brevity]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             
[30] "Latexmk: Log file says output to 'test.pdf'"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         
[31] "Latexmk: All targets () are up-to-date"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              
[32] ""   
```

## Setting `stdout` and `stderr` to pipes 

Causes the process to hang indefinitely:

```r
# Cleanup for next run
pc <- processx::process$new(command = "latexmk", args = c("-C"))
pc$wait()
if (file.exists("test.pdf")) file.remove("test.pdf")

p <- processx::process$new(
  command = "latexmk", args = c("-pdf", "test.tex"),
  stderr = "|",
  stdout = "|",
  echo_cmd = TRUE
)

# Hangs seemingly forever
p$wait()
```

## Setting `stdout` and `stderr` to pipes with `latexmk -C`

It's specifically this compilation that's the issue, because piping with e.g. `latexmk -C` works fine:

```r
p <- processx::process$new(
  command = "latexmk", args = c("-C"),
  stderr = "|",
  stdout = "|",
  echo_cmd = TRUE
)

p$wait()
```

```r

title: redirection of stdout in subjob
description:
I have a failure in a process that is started via `process$new('dumper',stdout='|') `that only happens with stdout sent to a pipe.  If I take off the `stdout` arg things work OK.  Perhaps this is an issue with processx that can be addressed.  Or perhaps I am doing something wrong with my dumper code.  Any insights or help appreciated.

The executable `dumper.exe` calls a windows batch file `dd.cmd`, and the batch file redirects stdout to a file.  Calling `dumper.exe` from a Windows command prompt works, but calling it as below fails:
```
p = process$new('dumper',stdout='|')
p$read_output()
[1] "dumper:  inheritHandles=0  useStdHandles=0  \r\n exitcode: 1 \r\n"
```
The redirection inside the cmd file fails: this is reflected in the exitcode of 1.  If I adjust dumper.c to run with inheritHandles=TRUE and leave the USESTDHANDLES bit alone, it works as hoped.  But for other reasons we want to run with inheritHandles=FALSE.

[dumper.c.txt](https://github.com/r-lib/processx/files/10550099/dumper.c.txt)

The content of dd.cmd:
```
@echo off
echo DD %1 %2 > dd.txt

```

title: Different behaviour inside and outside functions
description:
When I try to read output of `ls` from the global environment, it works fine, when I do exactly the same thing within a function defined in the global environment, I get no output.

``` r
library(processx)

p <- process$new("ls", stdin = "|", stdout = "|", stderr = "|")
my_output <- p$read_output()
p$kill()
#> [1] FALSE
my_output
#> [1] "mid-guppy_reprex.R\nmid-guppy_reprex.spin.R\nmid-guppy_reprex.spin.Rmd\n"

my_fun <- function(){
  local_p <- process$new("ls", stdin = "|", stdout = "|", stderr = "|")
  local_output <- local_p$read_output()
  local_p$kill()
  local_output
}

my_fun()
#> [1] ""
```

title: errno is modified in signal handlers
description:
Using [thread sanitizer](https://github.com/google/sanitizers/wiki/ThreadSanitizerDetectableBugs) I found that the signal handler for SIGCHLD `processx__sigchld_callback` https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/8a959afb25edb5d8eacd8e30e429a6f78b556aac/src/unix/sigchld.c#L41

may modify `errno`. The fix is to save `errno` when entering and restoring it when exiting the signal handler, like in `processx.c`

https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/b7e15fb62758de25f7ed9cc9ceb437f10d6362a3/src/unix/processx.c#L92

I am happy to send a PR, but it's unclear to me yet on how to best write an automated test for it.

title: Is it expected that passing a file path to `stdout` doesn't respect `wd`?
description:
``` r
library(processx)
# Set up a simple file structure
run("mkdir", "test_dir") -> x
run("touch", "test_file_1") -> x
run("touch", "test_dir/test_file_2") -> x
# Try to run ls inside the created directory
run("ls", wd = "test_dir", stdout = "ls_out") -> x
cat(run("ls")$stdout)
#> ls_out
#> test_dir
#> test_file_1
```

This was a surprising behaviour to me when I realised what was happening. Passing the output of the command to a file using the `stdout` argument does not respect the `wd` setting. In this situation, I had expected the file `ls_out` to be written to inside `test_dir`, rather than in the working directory as actually happens.

I could see this either way. On the one hand, I was using this as a drop in replacement for `cd test_dir; ls > ls_out`, where `ls_out` is clearly written to `test_dir`. On the other hand, it makes some sense that the `stdout` argument should be in reference to the working directory of the user calling `run()`, not the process being created. I think a brief documentation mention might help clear this up?

title: `run()` tries to execute the wrong command on Windows if there is a space in `command` and `args`
description:
This is an issue that we found in qgisprocess ( https://github.com/paleolimbot/qgisprocess/issues/36 ), the executable for which is a .bat file whose path almost always contains a space (C:/Program Files/...). When operating on a file with a space in it, `processx::run()` reports that `C:/Program` does not exist. I can reproduce this on Windows with an arbitrary batchfile name with a space as well using development processx:

``` r
library(processx)

tmp_dir <- tempfile()
dir.create(tmp_dir)
command_with_space <- file.path(tmp_dir, "has space.bat")
write("dir", command_with_space)
command_without_space <- file.path(tmp_dir, "nospace.bat")
write("dir", command_without_space)

run(
  command_with_space,
  "argwithoutspace"
)$status
#> [1] 0

run(
  command_without_space,
  args = "arg with space"
)$status
#> [1] 0

run(
  command_with_space,
  args = "arg with space"
)$status
#> Error in run(command_with_space, args = "arg with space"): System command 'has space.bat' failed, exit status: 1, stderr:
#> E> 'C:\Users\DUNNIN~1\AppData\Local\Temp\1\RtmpMxoryK\file28e8f9aad5/has' is not recognized as an internal or external command,
#> E> operable program or batch file.
```

title: Not possible to combine commands?

In pure command line, I would do something along the lines:

From within R, I try assembling the same command like this:

```
library(processx)
process$new("touch", c("test1.txt", "&&", "touch", "test2.txt"))
```

But it doesn't work as expected. It creates files `test1.txt`, `&&`, `touch` and `test2.txt`, whereas I would expect only `test1.txt` and `test2.txt` to be created.

What am I missing? Is this something I can achieve with `processx`?

title: Allow PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD to be set after processx is loaded?
description:
From #237:

>This is now opt in, and the PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD env var has to be set (to any value), at the time of loading of the processx package.

Are there plans to relax the restriction about setting the env var before loading `processx`? This would help unit testing for packages that depend on `processx`. For `targets`, I need to set `PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD=true` in `~/.Renviron` to avoid "Error while shutting down parallel: unable to terminate some child processes". `Sys.setenv(PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD = "true")` in the package's `.onLoad()` or `tests/testthat.R` is already too late.

Somewhat related: https://github.com/mschubert/clustermq/discussions/266

title: Race condition for `wd` if R changes wd quickly after starting subprocess
description:
```r
getwd()
#> [1] "/data/code/forks/reprex"
normalizePath(getwd())
#> [1] "/data/code/forks/reprex"
callr::r(function() getwd())
#> [1] "/data/code/forks/reprex"
callr::r(function() normalizePath(getwd()))
#> [1] "/data/code/forks/reprex"

withr::with_dir (tempdir(), {
                     c (getwd(),
                        normalizePath(getwd()),
                        callr::r(function() getwd()),
                        callr::r(function() normalizePath(getwd())))
          })
#> [1] "/tmp/RtmpLaG51T"              "/tmp/RtmpLaG51T"             
#> [3] "/data/code/forks/reprex" "/data/code/forks/reprex"
```

The possible fix is to pass wd explicitly to the C code and the child process, instead of letting `fork()` copy if from the main process.

title: `run()$stdout` is missing characters on Linux when multi-byte unicode characters are included in the output
description:
This doesn't happen on MacOS or Windows, but does on at least Ubuntu focal (I'm using rocker/ubuntu:20.04 here):

``` r
processx::run("echo", "\U00E9.1234")$stdout
#> [1] "é.1234"
processx::run("echo", "\U00E9\U00E9.1234")$stdout
#> [1] "éé.123"
processx::run("echo", "\U00E9\U00E9\U00E9.1234")$stdout
#> [1] "ééé.12"
```

Using a stdout callback seems to return the correct result:

``` r
result <- ""
px_res <- processx::run(
  "echo", "\U00E9\U00E9\U00E9.1234",
  stdout_callback = function(x, ...) {
    result <<- paste0(result, x)
  }
)
 
result
#> [1] "ééé.1234\n"
```

title: Windows: execution in background and cleanup
description:
Hi,
I'm using processx on windows and I'm experiencing the following problem.

I've created a dummy test file, named test_process.R, containing only the following lines:

for (i in 1:60){
   print(i)
   Sys.sleep(1)
}

Then I try to source it using Rscript via processx, redirecting stdout and stderr on two separated files. I repeat the line twice, once specifying "cleanup=TRUE", once "cleanup=FALSE".

require(processx)
myrscript<-paste0(R.home(),"/bin/Rscript")
myproc1<-process$new(myrscript, "test_process.R",stdout="test1_out.txt",stderr="test1_err.txt",cleanup=TRUE)
myproc2<-process$new(myrscript, "test_process.R",stdout="test2_out.txt",stderr="test2_err.txt",cleanup=FALSE)

The first process runs in background and the stdout is correctly redirected on "test1_out.txt".
The second process runs in foreground in a new window and the file "test2_out.txt" is created but remains empty.

Is this an expected behaviour? How can I prevent the cleanup but run in background?
I'd like to report that on ubuntu and OSX this does not happen.

I attach the zip file with the two dummy R files, for reference.

title: Launch process with default environment, without inheritance
description:
## Ask
By default, `env=NULL` when launching `process$new()` means that the subprocess inherits the parent's envirnoment. I'm looking for an easy way to launch a subprocess as if it was launched from the OS directly. 

## Context
I'm trying to launch RScript commands from one version of R interactively, to launch R sessions in other R versions. This is very error prone since the R-version-specific user library (R_LIBS_USER) is passed down to the other R sessions. 

## Workaround
I tried passing an empty vector like `env=c()` but found this has the same effects as `env=NULL`. 
I found that passing a dummy variable overwrites the behavior `env=c(zzzzz = "dummy")` and correctly resets the environment to more or less the "default"

title: Client lib: need to close dup()-d file handle when redirecting stdout/stderr
description:
``` r
library(processx)

ps::ps_open_files(ps::ps_handle())
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      fd path                                                                    
#>   <int> <chr>                                                                   
#> 1     0 /dev/null                                                               
#> 2     3 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/Rtmpi8bMzs/cal…

tmp <- tempfile()
con <- conn_create_file(tmp, read = FALSE, write = TRUE)
ps::ps_open_files(ps::ps_handle())
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      fd path                                                                    
#>   <int> <chr>                                                                   
#> 1     0 /dev/null                                                               
#> 2     3 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/Rtmpi8bMzs/cal…
#> 3     4 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/RtmpNNsTS9/fil…
```

We'll redirect stderr to the new fd 4.

``` r
old <- processx::conn_set_stderr(con, drop = FALSE)
ps::ps_open_files(ps::ps_handle())
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>      fd path                                                                    
#>   <int> <chr>                                                                   
#> 1     0 /dev/null                                                               
#> 2     2 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/RtmpNNsTS9/fil…
#> 3     3 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/Rtmpi8bMzs/cal…
#> 4     4 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/RtmpNNsTS9/fil…
```

stderr (fd 2) is now going to the new file, but fd 4 is still open.  The redirection should close it, I think. At least the version that is in the client lib.

``` r
processx:::close.processx_connection(con)
#> NULL
ps::ps_open_files(ps::ps_handle())
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      fd path                                                                    
#>   <int> <chr>                                                                   
#> 1     0 /dev/null                                                               
#> 2     2 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/RtmpNNsTS9/fil…
#> 3     3 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/Rtmpi8bMzs/cal…

cat("hello\n", file = stderr())

processx::conn_set_stderr(old, drop = TRUE)
ps::ps_open_files(ps::ps_handle())
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      fd path                                                                    
#>   <int> <chr>                                                                   
#> 1     0 /dev/null                                                               
#> 2     3 /private/var/folders/59/0gkmw1yj2w7bf2dfc3jznv5w0000gn/T/Rtmpi8bMzs/cal…

readLines(tmp)
#> [1] "hello"
```

title: UTF-8 path fails in older R versions, on Windows
Non-ascii arguments in the native encoding are garbled on Windows
description:
Because processx assumes that they are in UTF-8. R 4.0.2, Windows 10:

ASCII app:

```r
local_temp_dir()
name <- enc2native("\u00fa\u00e1\u00f6")

out <- run(get_tool("px"), c("writefile", "of", name))
expect_equal(
    charToRaw(name),
    readBin("of", what = "raw", n = 100)
)
#> Error: charToRaw(name) not equal to readBin("of", what = "raw", n = 100).
#> 3 element mismatches
```
Unicode app:

```r
out2 <- run(get_tool("pxu"), c("writefile", "of2", name))
expect_equal(
    iconv(name, to = "UCS-2LE", toRaw = TRUE)[[1]],
    readBin("of2", what = "raw", n = 100)
)
#> Error: iconv(name, to = "UCS-2LE", toRaw = TRUE)[[1]] not equal to readBin("of2", what = "raw", n = 100).
#> 6 element mismatches
```

And I consistently get:

Type .Last.error.trace to see where the error occured
```

I was told to try this rather simple processx command:

`> process$new("dir", "hello", supervise = TRUE)`

Which outputs a similar error.

```
Error in rethrow_call(c_processx_exec, command, c(command, args), stdin,  :

```

I reinstalled processx in a new R session, but same error. So I manually uninstalled from RStudio and reinstalled again, but same thing.

I wonder whether it could be due to my username having spaces and accents (though I cannot change it). I know it has given me some trouble with other packages in the past.

title: Occasional NA returned by get_exit_status
description:
Hello,

On my Linux box (OpenSUSE) on some occasions the `get_exit_status()` function may return `NA` after execution of a (successful) command. I'm mainly using this function to check if the command executed without problems. I typically notice this when a long batch (~50-100) of commands are executed in chunks, each launched by process$new(). So far it mainly seems when executing Java commands, but this might be coincidence. 

I'm not using `mcparallel` and as far as I can tell none of the dependent packages use `SIGCHLD` handlers. Still I am unsure about this and I was wondering if there would be a way to easily check this. 

Thanks,
Rick

title: run hangs with mpiexec
description:
On Ubuntu 18.04 with OpenMPI (just the default configuration installed from the package manager), I can run this command from the command line:

```
:/$ mpiexec ls
bin    dev   initrd.img      lib32	 media	proc  sbin  sys  var
boot   etc   initrd.img.old  lib64	 mnt	root  snap  tmp  vmlinuz
...
```

However if I run the same thing in processx it hangs after executing the command (it never returns control to R):

```
processx::run(command = "mpiexec", args = "ls", echo = TRUE)
```

If I run this with process$new I can check is_alive and it stays TRUE.

I can run this with system and it executes and returns control:

```
system("mpiexec ls")
```

Any ideas about what might be happening? I'm not entirely sure how this works, and since mpiexec is forking processes to run in parallel it seems reasonable that it might be messing something up so processx isn't able to detect what is going on. Any tips would be appreciated!

title: Cannot pipe to a file from processx::run()
description:
Thanks for this awesome project! We're starting to use it in [LightGBM](https://github.com/microsoft/LightGBM) to get around the overhead introduced by `system()` and `system2()`.

In the docs for `?processx::run`, I see this:

> ...	
Extra arguments are passed to process$new(), see process.

In `?procesxx::process`, I see the argument `stdout`, with this description:

> What to do with the standard output. Possible values: NULL: discard it; a string, redirect it to this file; "|": create a connection for it.

Given that, I expected to be able pass `stdout` as a keyword argument to get `processx::run()` to write to a file.

```r
processx::run(
    command = "ls"
    , stdout = "file.txt"
)
```

This doesn't work, though. It results in the following error:

> Error in processx::run(command = "ls", stdout = "file.txt") : 
  argument 2 matches multiple formal arguments

I think this is because of fuzzy argument name matching in R. `stdout` is being matched to all of the `stdout_*` arguments in `processx::run()`.

Is there another way to get `processx::run()` to pipe stdout to a file? If not I'll drop down to the `process` object. Thanks!

title: Error while shutting down parallel: unable to terminate some child processes
description:
As discussed in #113, there seems to be an interaction between `parallel::mclapply` and `processx` related to a signal handler. 

The symptom is this message when leaving a R session or entering debug:
`Error while shutting down parallel: unable to terminate some child processes`

It also comes with a noticeable delay to quit or enter the debug session. 

I could not manage to build a reproducible example yet.
And actually I do not use **processx** directly but **callr**.

title: Converting a commandline string into processx::run args
description:
Often, it's easier/more intuitive to provide the input options to a program as a full string:

    --arg1 --arg2 "here is a sentence" "/path/to/file with spaces"

However, processx expects each option to be a separate element in a vector of strings:

    c("--arg1", "--arg2", "here is a sentence", "/path/to/file with spaces")

Is there a good/recommended way of going from the first to the second? Simply using `strsplit` to split on spaces will fail on the input here, since it will also break up the inputs that have spaces in them.

title: Dynamically updated output with `run`
description:
It would be nice if `run` had better support for programs that continually update the screen. Taking the example of docker again:

- `system2("docker", "pull <foo>")` prints the status updates to the screen as they occur, with progress bars that update properly. It mimics what you'd see if you ran docker from the commandline.
- `processx::run("docker", c("pull", "<foo>"), echo=TRUE)` doesn't show the progress bars at all, and only shows the updated status as each layer operation completes.

title: Zombies when processx (via callr) and parallel are used in the same session.
description:
The [`drake`](https://github.com/ropensci/drake) package tries to be a high-performance computing engine, so it includes some small unit tests of its parallel backends. In R 3.5.0, when I run these tests with `test_check()` or `devtools::test()`, I see a bunch of zombie processes when I call `top -bn1 | grep R$` in a Linux shell. Then, when I quit the R session, I see "Error while shutting down parallel: unable to terminate some child processes". This does not seem to happen if I use `devtools::check()` or revert to R 3.4.4.

The tests use `callr` and `parallel` at various points, though never in the same test. If I run each test in a separate R session, or if I deactivate only the uses of `callr`, there are no zombies.

title: Never ends without reading output when running a process in the background on macOS
description:
Thanks for this amazing package. I encountered an issue when calling an external program [EnergyPlus](https://energyplus.net) in the background.

```r
# for EnergyPlus program
remotes::install_github('hongyuanjia/eplusr')
eplusr::install_eplus(8.8, local = TRUE)
```

Everything works fine when directly calling EnergyPlus using `processx::run`.

``` r
s <- Sys.time()
job <- processx::run(eplusr:::eplus_exe(8.8),
    c(
        "--weather",
        normalizePath(file.path(eplusr::eplus_config(8.8)$dir, "WeatherData/USA_CA_San.Francisco.Intl.AP.724940_TMY3.epw")),
        "--output-directory",
        tempdir(),
        "--annual",
        normalizePath(file.path(eplusr::eplus_config(8.8)$dir, "ExampleFiles/RefBldgLargeOfficeNew2004_Chicago.idf"))
    )
)
e <- Sys.time()
difftime(e, s)
#> Time difference of 41.03216 secs
```

And also `processx::process$new` when output are polled using `$read_output_lines()`.

```r
s <- Sys.time()
job <- processx::process$new(eplusr:::eplus_exe(8.8),
    c(
        "--weather",
        normalizePath(file.path(eplusr::eplus_config(8.8)$dir, "WeatherData/USA_CA_San.Francisco.Intl.AP.724940_TMY3.epw")),
        "--output-directory",
        tempdir(),
        "--annual",
        normalizePath(file.path(eplusr::eplus_config(8.8)$dir, "ExampleFiles/RefBldgLargeOfficeNew2004_Chicago.idf"))
    ),
    stdout = "|", stderr = "|"
)
while(job$is_alive()) {
    Sys.sleep(1)
    job$read_output_lines(100)
}
e <- Sys.time()
difftime(e, s)
#> Time difference of 40.10853 secs
```

<sup>Created on 2020-01-26 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

However, without polling output, the background process never ends.

```r
s <- Sys.time()
job <- processx::process$new(eplusr:::eplus_exe(8.8),
    c(
        "--weather",
        normalizePath(file.path(eplus_config(8.8)$dir, "WeatherData/USA_CA_San.Francisco.Intl.AP.724940_TMY3.epw")),
        "--output-directory",
        tempdir(),
        "--annual",
        normalizePath(file.path(eplus_config(8.8)$dir, "ExampleFiles/RefBldgLargeOfficeNew2004_Chicago.idf"))
    ),
    stdout = "|", stderr = "|"
)
# never ends...
while(job$is_alive()) Sys.sleep(1)
e <- Sys.time()
difftime(e, s)
```

Any insights? Thanks!

title: Spinner not showing up
description:
Hi,

I am running R GUI version 3.6.0 on Windows 10. While my problem stems from trying to use callr::r() with the spinner, I have tracked the problem down to  [the spin() function](https://github.com/r-lib/processx/blob/88437067f84bc27b3d01da05bfdf3714f33d9689/R/run.R#L278), defined inside the function run_manage().

As an example, running the code below (from the demo code in the readme) will not produce a spinner.

```r
px <- paste0(
  system.file(package = "processx", "bin", "px"),
  system.file(package = "processx", "bin", .Platform$r_arch, "px.exe")
)

result <- run(px,
  c("out", "  foo",
    "sleep", "1",
    "out", "\r  bar",
	"sleep", "1",
	"out", "\rX foobar\n"),
  echo = TRUE, spinner = TRUE)
```


I have explored the run_manage function and I found that editing the spin function from:
```r
# Currently defined spin
  spin <- (function() {
    state <- 1L
    phases <- c("-", "\\", "|", "-")
    function() {
      cat("\r", phases[state], "\r", sep = "")
      state <<- (state + 1) %% length(phases) + 1L
    }
  })()
```
to:
```r
# spin function edited by me
spin <- (function() {
  state <- 1L
  phases <- c("-", "\\", "|", "/")
  function() {
    cat("\r", phases[state], "\r", sep = "")
    state <<- (state)%%length(phases) + 1L
    flush.console() 
  }
})()
```
solves the issue. 

Specifically, adding the flush.console() line solves the issue: the spinner shows up and rolls in place as expected.

I took the chance to fix an additional issue where the spinner phases were not showing up in the correct order, by changing the lines starting with "phases <- ..." "state <<- ..." (see above).

This is the first time I am posting an issue in someone's repository, so I hope I am not breaking any formality (apologies if I am).

Thanks for any help you can give me!
Hugo

title: run() with stdin
description:
Is it possible to add `stdin` to `run()` (as done with `process$new()` and #27)?

An example where it'd be nice to use `run()`'s built-in synchronous process management is something like calling pandoc where `stdin` is a string and we can capture `stdout` directly into an output string. Ways to do this now include writing some wrapping management around `process$new()` (effectively rewriting some of `run()`'s functionality) or writing the input string to a file and calling pandoc on that file, then deleting the file, which seems clunky.

Either way, thanks much for `processx`; very useful!

title: Better errors in `run()`
description:
In general, if something fails, we should have some reasonable defaults as to what to do with `stderr`, both in `run()`.

E.g. this is not very helpful:
```

Error in run("R", c("CMD", "build", "/tmp"), echo = TRUE) :

```

Maybe `run()` should default to `echo = TRUE`?

title: Fix crash on Windows
description: This one: https://ci.appveyor.com/project/gaborcsardi/processx/builds/23541945#L553

title: Win: do IO in another thread
description: Because a thread can only work with one IOCP and R or other packages might create IOCPs from the main thread.

title: Fix Windows crash when getting reply from wrong async read in IOCP
description:
In theory this happens when the same thread creates multiple IOCPs, and indeed R-devel uses IOCPs now: https://github.com/wch/r-source/commit/fd4545643221862555559da9f296e3f996bfc567
However it also happens in R 3.5.2, I have no idea why.

Anyway, what happens is that `GetQueuedCompletionStatus()` returns with a `key` that was not added by processx, and then of course processx crashes.

Ideally, we would run the poll/read in another thread, but for a quick workaround, we should just ignore events that are not coming from processx.

title: Small tip: making sure processes exit after user interrupt
description:
Hello,

Not a bug report, just an FYI as I couldn't find anything about this elsewhere (please correct me if I'm wrong though!).

At the moment (sub)processes are not cleaned up after user interruption (e.g. pressing the 'stop' button). A simple workaround is to wrap the code in `tryCatch` and call `gc()` in case an interruption occurs:
```R
tryCatch(doYourProcessxThing(), interrupt = function(e) gc(verbose = FALSE))

# or to suppress output from gc()
tryCatch(doYourProcessxThing(), interrupt = function(e) invisible(capture.output(gc(verbose = FALSE))))
```

Cheers,
Rick

title: warn users run(args = ) cannot include spaces
description:
Let's say I want to run `ls -a -l`.

Obviously, this is not the same as `ls '-a -l'` (that errors out, because the flags are not treated as, well, flags).

I ran myself into circles by doing something boneheaded like this:

```
processx::run(command = "ls", args = "-a -l", echo_cmd = TRUE)
```

which runs the command `Running ls '-a -l'` and deservedly fails.

I (kinda, sorta?) understand why this was stupid on my part (probably the escaping by `base::shQuote()`).

However, I got confused, because `system2()` *behaves differently*.

```
system2(command = "ls", args = '-a -l')
```

will actually **work**!

I understand this might be related to [this bug in system2](https://bugs.r-project.org/bugzilla3/show_bug.cgi?id=16127), and anyway, that processx is supposed to be better than this.

Still, I wondered whether other people might also run into this, transitioning from `system2()` to `processx::run()`, and so might benefit from a warning in the docs.

If you agree, I'll try and add a short PR to that effect.





I understand (maybe? a little?) why this behavior is necessary to

title: poll() works only if stdout or stderr is pipe
description:
For example:

```R
p <- processx::process$new("sleep", "5", stdout="|")
poll(list(p), 10000)  # Waits for 5 seconds


p <- processx::process$new("sleep", "5")
poll(list(p), 10000)  # Returns immediately
```

It also doesn't work when stdout is written to a file, which is my current use case.

The help says:
> poll() cannot wait on the termination of a process directly. It is only signalled through the closed stdout and stderr pipes. 

Couldn't it actually poll to see if the processes are still running?

If it's not possible to make `poll()` work when stdout isn't a pipe, then it be helpful to:

description:

```R
  old_dir <- setwd(new_dir)
  # In case we have an error in process$new(), use on.exit
  on.exit(setwd(old_dir))
  p <- process$new("ls", stdout = "|")$wait()
  setwd(old_dir)
```

title: Rewrite I/O using IOCP
description:
It will make polling easier, probably.

EDIT 2017-11-06

Initially I did not do this, because I did not see how I could poll a certain _subset_ of processes or pipes (but _not_ poll the rest of the processes/pipes on the same IOCP). But this is easy if we implement buffering, which we already do. We can just poll the IOCP with all processes, and if a read finishes on a process/pipe that we are not polling on, we just put the data in the buffer, and continue polling. We do not restart the read for the processes that we are not polling, obviously.

IOCP is also good, because currently we have a limit for polling maximum 64 handles, this is a limit of `WaitForMultipleObjects` that is very hard to go around.

title: Quoted command on Windows fails to start process
description:
On Windows, if there are quotes around the command (when using `commandline`), then it fails to start the process correctly. Or at least the process exits with an error. For example:

```R
library(processx)
p <- process$new(commandline = "echo abc")
p$get_exit_status() # 0

p <- process$new(commandline = '"echo" abc')
Sys.sleep(0.25)
p$get_exit_status() # 1

# Works fine with system()
system('"echo" abc') # abc
```

title: Remove support for `commandline`?
description:
It is just not possible to remove the child tree on `$kill()`, so using an intermediate shell might leave processes behind.

On windows the situation is even worse, because not only is the child process of the shell left behind, the `stdout` and `stderr` pipes are also not closed when the shell exits.

So it would be cleaner to remove `commandline` altogether. If you need a shell, you can always call one directly.

title: supervisor_kill can leave behind zombies
description:
Running `supervisor_kill()` can leave behind zombie processes, on both Mac and Linux:

```R
library(processx)
process$new('sleep', args='1000', commandline=NULL, cleanup=F, supervise=T)
process$new('sleep', args='1000', commandline=NULL, cleanup=F, supervise=T)
process$new('sleep', args='1000', commandline=NULL, cleanup=F, supervise=T)
process$new('sleep', args='1000', commandline=NULL, cleanup=F, supervise=T)
process$new('sleep', args='1000', commandline=NULL, cleanup=F, supervise=T)
processx:::supervisor_kill()
```

Running `ps` after the R code above:

```
$ ps aux | grep sleep
winston          60850   0.0  0.0        0      0   ??  Z     4:33PM   0:00.00 (sleep)
winston          60848   0.0  0.0        0      0   ??  Z     4:33PM   0:00.00 (sleep)
winston          60862   0.0  0.0  2432804   2000 s004  S+    4:34PM   0:00.00 grep sleep
```

`supervisor_kill()` usually runs only when R exits, and so it won't leave behind zombie processes, but even so, this should not happen.

When `supervisor_kill()` is called, this code that sends SIGTERMs is run: https://github.com/r-pkgs/processx/blob/a60d83a/src/supervisor/supervisor.c#L144-L153


Is it possible that this is happening because the SIGCHLD events are coming very close together and the SIGCHLD handler can't handle them that quickly?

```

p <- process$new('sleep', '1000', cleanup=F, commandline=NULL)

title: Send interrupt (hard on windows)
description:

On unix/macos this can be implemented as

```r
process_interrupt <- function(self, private) {
    "!DEBUG process_interrupt '`private$get_short_name()`', pid `private$pid`"
    if (!is.null(private$pid)) {
        pids <- c(private$pid, get_pid_tree(private$pid))
        pskill(pids, SIGINT)
    }
    invisible(self)
}
```

```
